Arguing about whether or not human-driven climate change is occurring is a waste of energy. The focus of the human-impact-on-the-planet discussions should focus instead on the total toxification of the environment. The fact that we are filling the air, water, and soil with pollutants is not up for debate. We can see the smog, the spills, the dirty river, the side of the road. The impacts of this pollution are more tangible than long term climate change, and thus more real to the average person. We can see the plastic in the seagull's belly, but we can't see the future. The only reason that climate change grips so tightly to the cultural consciousness is because the facts have been transformed into belief. Only a small percentage of us are able to interpret climate data, the rest have to use our best judgement in trusting those who say they can. So the argument has shifted into character judgements, as opposed to what is actually happening. Turning the conversation about healing the planet from climate change to pollution has several benefits in terms of potential to affect action: there is no debate about whether or not we are polluting the air, water, and soil; pollution is occurring now, not in a far off maybe; we can see, touch, taste, and smell the pollution; it is killing us faster than climate change (for the time being); and finally, addressing net pollution includes dealing with greenhouse gases, so nothing is lost in the fight against climate change.

Basically, climate change is a distraction that trumps other discussions without being able to be resolved. That, and we very well may have already passed the point-of-no-return for catastrophic climate change anyway.

What to do:

Call and e-mail your representatives, share and etc.: https://savetheinternet.eu

Deadline - Tuesday, October 27!

Summary:

The European Union was going to have one of the strongest net neutrality rules in the world, but it all went down the drain when in the late June they caved to ISPs and reached "a compromise", that is in reality a weak mish-mash of rules that allow for discrimination of the traffic and fast lanes and way less stronger that the ones adopted by USA.

List of problem includes:

1) Fast lanes (hiding under the name of "specialized services");

2) Zero-rating (not banned discriminatory practice);

3) Discrimination of the traffic by its type (class-based discrimination for "optimizing" networks - innovation killer) EDIT4: - online video games will suffer from it (see "More information"). There is also a possible discrimination against encrypted traffic.

4) Rules that allow to prevent "impending" congestions - basically, slow down the traffic whenever ISP want.

But there are amendments to the EU net neutrality law available that can fix mentioned problems with it, and there is a campaign to call (preferable!), e-mail and message EU Parliament representatives to adopt those amendments on October 27 - https://savetheinternet.eu

More information:

A really good article that probably will answer all of your questions: article, (archive).

EDIT3: Video games related quotes:

For example, many ISPs in the UK limit the bandwidth available to peer-to-peer file sharing applications during times of congestion, arguing that these applications are not sensitive to delay. This creates huge problems for online gaming. ISPs use deep packet inspection technology to identify these applications, but the technology doesn’t work very well: it has a hard time distinguishing between online gaming and peer-to-peer file sharing, so online games stop working or don’t work as well as they could.

If an online gaming provider wants to introduce a new feature for its game in the UK, it needs to work with the ISPs and their technology vendors to make sure that the feature won’t be caught up in the traffic management measures directed at peer-to-peer file sharing. This is the opposite of innovation without permission.

Just quotes:

Unless it adopts amendments, the European Parliament’s net neutrality vote next Tuesday threatens the open Internet in Europe.

...

If a majority of the members who vote approves this flawed compromise next Tuesday, the rules are adopted and become law. Europe will have far weaker network neutrality rules than the US, and the European Internet would become less free and less open. By contrast, if a majority of the members approves amendments, the text goes back to the Council. The Council can then accept the amendments, and they become law. If the Council rejects the amendments, a joint committee consisting of representatives of the Parliament and the Council has six weeks to come up with a compromise. Any compromise would then have to be adopted by the Parliament and the Council.

The future of the Internet in Europe is on the line. It’s up to all of us to save it.
